claim: The human endogenous retrovirus type-H (HERVH) family is expressed in the preimplantation embryo.
source: The human endogenous retrovirus type-H (HERVH) family is expressed in the preimplantation embryo.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about HERVH expression.

claim: A subset of HERVH elements are specifically transcribed in pluripotent stem cells where they appear to exert regulatory activities promoting self-renewal and pluripotency.
source: A subset of these elements are specifically transcribed in pluripotent stem cells where they appear to exert regulatory activities promoting self-renewal and pluripotency.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to previous literature throughout the manuscript.

claim: The LTR7 family includes at least eight previously unrecognized subfamilies that have been active at different timepoints in primate evolution.
source: We found that the family includes at least eight previously unrecognized subfamilies that have been active at different timepoints in primate evolution and display distinct expression patterns during human embryonic development.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B and dating analysis in Figure 2.

claim: Nearly all HERVH elements transcribed in ESCs belong to the LTR7up subfamily.
source: Notably, nearly all HERVH elements transcribed in ESCs belong to one of the youngest subfamilies we dubbed LTR7up.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-seq and GRO-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: LTR7 sequence evolution was driven by a mixture of mutational processes, including point mutations, duplications, and multiple recombination events between subfamilies.
source: LTR7 sequence evolution was driven by a mixture of mutational processes, including point mutations, duplications, and multiple recombination events between subfamilies, that led to transcription factor binding motif modules characteristic of each subfamily.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment and parsimony tree analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: A predicted SOX2/3 binding site unique to LTR7up is essential for robust promoter activity in induced pluripotent stem cells.
source: Using a reporter assay, we show that one such motif, a predicted SOX2/3 binding site unique to LTR7up, is essential for robust promoter activity in induced pluripotent stem cells.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Many TEs have evolved stage-specific expression in germ cells or early embryonic development.
source: To this end, many TEs have evolved stage-specific expression in germ cells or early embryonic development (Faulkner et al., 2009; Fort et al., 2014; Göke et al., 2015; Miao et al., 2020; Urusov et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Many endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) exhibit highly stage-specific expression during early embryonic development.
source: Many endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) are known to exhibit highly stage-specific expression during early embryonic development (Chang et al., 2021; Göke et al., 2015; Hermant and Torres-Padilla, 2021; Peaston et al., 2004; Svoboda et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: HERVH is a family derived from a gamma retrovirus that first entered the genome of the common ancestor of apes, Old World monkeys (OWMs), and New World monkeys more than 40 million years ago.
source: One of the most abundant families is HERVH, a family derived from a gamma retrovirus that first entered the genome of the common ancestor of apes, Old World monkeys (OWMs), and New World monkeys more than 40 million years ago (mya) (Goodchild et al., 1993; Izsvák et al., 2016; Mager and Freeman, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: No polymorphic HERVH insertions have been found in the human genome.
source: To date, no polymorphic HERVH insertions have been found in the human genome (Thomas et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: There are four subfamilies of HERVH elements currently recognized in the Dfam and Repbase databases: LTR7, 7b, 7c, and 7y.
source: There are four subfamilies of HERVH elements currently recognized in the Dfam (Storer et al., 2021) and Repbase (Bao et al., 2015; Kojima, 2018) databases and annotated in the reference human genome based on distinct LTR consensus sequences: LTR7 (formerly known as Type I), 7b (Type II), 7c, and 7y (Type Ia) (Bao et al., 2015; Goodchild et al., 1993; Jern et al., 2005; Jern et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to databases and previous literature.

claim: Family-wide HERVH knockdown results in the loss of pluripotency of human ESC and reduced reprogramming efficiency of somatic cells to iPSC.
source: Several studies showed that family-wide HERVH knockdown results in the loss of pluripotency of human ESC and reduced reprogramming efficiency of somatic cells to iPSC (Lu et al., 2014; Ohnuki et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Different HERVH knockdown constructs produced variable results and inconsistent phenotypes.
source: However, it is important to emphasize that different HERVH knockdown constructs produced variable results and inconsistent phenotypes (Lu et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2019), and a recent knockout experiment of the most highly transcribed locus (ESRG) failed to recapitulate its previous knockdown phenotype (Takahashi et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: HERVH expression in human ESCs, iPSCs, and the pluripotent epiblast can be attributed to a relatively small subset of loci (estimated between 83 and 209) driven by LTR7 sequences.
source: RNA-seq analyses have established that HERVH expression in human ESCs, iPSCs, and the pluripotent epiblast can be attributed to a relatively small subset of loci (estimated between 83 and 209) driven by LTR7 (sensu stricto) sequences (Göke et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous RNA-seq studies.

claim: LTR7 elements can be divided into eight subfamilies based on phylogenetic criteria.
source: Based on these criteria, LTR7 elements could be divided into eight subfamilies (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The subfamilies 7o, 7bc, and 7c are the oldest LTR7 subfamilies since the majority of their insertions are found at orthologous position in rhesus macaque.
source: The subfamilies 7o, 7bc, and 7c are the oldest since the majority of their insertions are found at orthologous position in rhesus macaque, an OWM.
evidence: This is supported by reciprocal liftover analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Most of the proliferation of 7o, 7bc, and 7c occurred prior to the split of OWM and hominoids, ~25 mya.
source: These three subfamilies share similar evolutionary trajectories, with most of their proliferation occurring prior to the split of OWM and hominoids, ~25 mya (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by reciprocal liftover analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Only 22% of human 7b elements could be lifted over to rhesus macaque and the vast majority appeared to have inserted between 10 and 20 mya.
source: Members of the 7b subfamily (the most numerous, 637 solo and full-length insertions) appear to be overall younger, since only 22% of the human 7b elements could be lifted over to rhesus macaque and the vast majority appeared to have inserted between 10 and 20 mya (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by reciprocal liftover analysis shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 7d1 and 7d2 subfamilies are largely hominoid-specific and achieved most of their proliferation prior to the split of African and Asian great apes ~14 mya.
source: Only 5 of the 550 elements in the 7d1 and 7d2 subfamilies could be retrieved in rhesus macaque, but ~30% were shared with gibbon and ~75% were shared with orangutan. Thus, these two subfamilies are largely hominoid-specific and achieved most of their proliferation prior to the split of African and Asian great apes ~14 mya (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by reciprocal liftover analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The 7up1/2, 7y, and 7u2 subfamilies represent the youngest in the human genome, with most of their proliferation occurring between ~10 and ~ 14 mya, in the ancestor of African great apes.
source: The 7up1/2, 7y, and 7u2 subfamilies represent the youngest in the human genome, with most of their proliferation occurring between ~10 and ~ 14 mya, in the ancestor of African great apes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by reciprocal liftover analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Only 14 of the 208 (6.7%) human 7up1 elements can be retrieved in orangutan, but 178 (85.6%) can be found in gorilla.
source: For example, only 14 of the 208 (6.7%) human 7up1 elements can be retrieved in orangutan, but 178 (85.6%) can be found in gorilla.
evidence: This is supported by reciprocal liftover analysis.

claim: Three major waves of HERVH propagation can be distinguished: an older wave 25–40 mya involving 7c, 7o, and 7bc elements, an intermediate wave 9–20 mya involving 7b, 7d1/2, and 7u1, and a most recent wave 4–10 mya implicating primarily 7up1/2, 7u2, and 7y elements.
source: Taken together, our dating analyses distinguish three major waves of HERV propagation: an older wave 25–40 mya involving 7c, 7o, and 7bc elements, an intermediate wave 9–20 mya involving 7b, 7d1/2, and 7u1, and a most recent wave 4–10 mya implicating primarily 7up1/2, 7u2, and 7y elements.
evidence: This is supported by both liftover analysis (Figure 2A) and terminal branch length analysis (Figure 2B).

claim: 33% of 7up elements (88 loci) are highly expressed according to RNA-seq compared with only 2% of highly expressed elements from all other subfamilies combined (17 loci).
source: Indeed, we estimated that 33% of 7up elements (88 loci) are highly expressed according to RNA-seq compared with only 2% of highly expressed elements from all other subfamilies combined (17 loci).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis from Wang et al., 2014.

claim: HERVH transcriptional activity in H1 ESCs is largely limited to loci driven by 7up sequences.
source: Thus, HERVH transcriptional activity in H1 ESCs is largely limited to loci driven by 7up sequences.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and GRO-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: KLF4 binding is a strong predictor of transcriptional activity: KLF4 ChIP-seq peaks overlap 91% of 7up loci.
source: As previously noted from ChIP-seq data (Ohnuki et al., 2014), we found that KLF4 binding is a strong predictor of transcriptional activity: KLF4 ChIP-seq peaks overlap 91% of 7up loci and KLF4 binding is strongly enriched for the 7up subfamilies relative to other subfamilies (Figure 3A, B, and D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: NANOG binding is enriched for 7up (97.7% of loci overlap ChIP-seq peaks) but is observed to varying degrees at other LTR7 loci that do not show evidence of active transcription.
source: NANOG binding is also enriched for 7up (97.7% of loci overlap ChIP-seq peaks) but is observed to varying degrees at other LTR7 loci that do not show evidence of active transcription based on GRO-seq and/or RNA-seq (85% of 7u1 loci, 32% 7d1, 45% 7d2, 13% 7o, 8.7% 7bc, and 0% of 7u2).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: OCT4 binds merely 12% of 7up loci.
source: While KLF4 and NANOG binding is pervasive across the 7up subfamily, OCT4 binds merely 12% of 7up loci.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: SOX2 binds 32% of LTR7up loci and 1–3% of all other LTR7 loci.
source: Other TFs with known roles in pluripotency are also enriched at 7up loci, such as SOX2 (32% LTR7up, 1–3% all other LTR7), FOXP1(49%, 0–4.3%), and FOXA1(28%, 0–1.4%).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: FOXA1 binds only a single non-7up insertion in the dataset, making it the most exclusive feature of 7up loci among the TFs examined.
source: In fact, FOXA1 binds only a single non-7up insertion in our dataset, making it the most exclusive feature of 7up loci among the TFs examined in this analysis (see Supplementary file 8 for full statistical analysis of all marks).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: 76% of LTR7up loci are decorated by H3K4me3, a mark of active promoters, compared to 19% of all other LTR7 loci.
source: Congruent with having generally more TF binding and transcriptional activity, 7up loci also have a propensity to be decorated by H3K4me3, a mark of active promoters (76% LTR7up vs. 19% all others) and the broader activity mark H3K27ac (89% vs. 48%) (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: 89% of LTR7up loci are decorated by H3K27ac compared to 48% of all other LTR7 loci.
source: Congruent with having generally more TF binding and transcriptional activity, 7up loci also have a propensity to be decorated by H3K4me3, a mark of active promoters (76% LTR7up vs. 19% all others) and the broader activity mark H3K27ac (89% vs. 48%) (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: H3K4me1, a mark typically associated with low POLII loading as seen at enhancers, is spread rather evenly throughout the tree of LTR7 sequences (26% vs. 18%).
source: By contrast, H3K4me1, a mark typically associated with low POLII loading as seen at enhancers as opposed to promoters, is spread rather evenly throughout the tree of LTR7 sequences (26% vs. 18%) (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: KAP1 and H3K9me3 loading were neither enriched nor depleted for 7up elements relative to other subfamilies.
source: We found that KAP1 and H3K9me3 loading were neither enriched nor depleted for 7up elements relative to other subfamilies (Figure 3A, C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: There were no significant differences in the level of H3K9me3 marking across subfamilies.
source: Overall, there were no significant differences in the level of H3K9me3 marking across subfamilies and the only difference in KAP1 binding was a slight but significant depletion for 7bc and 7o compared to all other subfamilies including 7up (14% vs. 35% – padj < 0.05 chi-square Bonferroni correction).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: KAP1 and H3K9me3 loading were found in similar proportions in expressed and unexpressed 7up elements (padj > 0.05).
source: Furthermore, KAP1 and H3K9me3 loading were found in similar proportions in expressed and unexpressed 7up elements (padj > 0.05) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CpG methylation was not differential between subfamilies (padj > 0.05).
source: This was also the case for CpG methylation, whose presence was not differential between subfamilies (padj > 0.05 Wilcoxon rank-sum with Bonferroni correction) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of WGBS-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: ZNF534 preferentially bound members of the 7up subfamily (72% of LTR7up vs. 34–53% of non-LTR7up).
source: We found that while ZNF90 bound all LTR7 subfamilies to a similar extent, ZNF534 preferentially bound members of the 7up subfamily (72% of LTR7up vs. 34–53% of non-LTR7up).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-exo data analysis from Imbeault et al., 2017.

claim: ZNF534 binding in 293 cells did not correlate with transcriptional activity of 7up elements in ESCs nor with KAP1 binding or H3K9me3 deposition in these cells.
source: However, ZNF534 binding in 293 cells did not correlate with transcriptional activity of 7up elements in ESCs nor with KAP1 binding or H3K9me3 deposition in these cells (Figure 3A, D).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of ChIP-exo and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: A minimum of six recombination events occurred between LTR7 subfamilies.
source: We found a minimum of six instances of clades supported in the block parsimony trees that were incongruent with those supported by the overall phylogeny (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This is supported by parsimony tree analysis of sequence blocks shown in Figure 4.

claim: The 7b subfamily exhibited expression at the 8 cell and morula stages, coinciding with EGA.
source: As previously observed (Göke et al., 2015), the 7b subfamily exhibited expression at the 8 cell and morula stages, coinciding with EGA (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The 7u2 subfamily expression was restricted to the pluripotent epiblast.
source: Another remarkable expression pattern was that of 7u2 which was restricted to the pluripotent epiblast (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The 7y subfamily combined the expression of 7b and 7u2 (8 cell and morula plus epiblast).
source: Interestingly, the 7y subfamily combined the expression of 7b and 7u2 (8 cell and morula plus epiblast), perhaps reflecting the acquisition of sequence blocks from both subfamilies (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5 and sequence analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: 7o elements show no significant transcription at any timepoint in early development, while 7bc elements display RNA expression throughout the blastocyst.
source: Despite very similar sequence and age (Figures 1, 2 and 4A), 7bc and 7o elements show stark contrast in their expression profiles. 7o elements show no significant transcription at any timepoint in early development, while 7bc elements display RNA expression throughout the blastocyst, including trophectoderm and inner cell mass, primitive endoderm, and pluripotent epiblast (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The single most striking motif distinguishing the 7up clade from the others was a SOX2/3 motif which coincided with an 8 bp insertion in block 2b.
source: Next, we sought to pinpoint mutational events responsible for the gain of TF motifs responsible for the unique expression of 7up in ESC. The single most striking motif distinguishing the 7up clade from the others was a SOX2/3 motif which coincided with an 8 bp insertion in block 2b (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6A and sequence alignment shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The 8 bp motif is present in 7u1, the closest relative to 7up, but absent in all other subfamilies.
source: Note this motif (and insertion) was also present in 7u1, the closest relative to 7up (Figure 1), but absent in all other subfamilies (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 6B and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: SOX2 and SOX3 bind a highly similar motif, activate an overlapping set of genes, and play a redundant function in pluripotency.
source: Indeed, SOX2 and SOX3 bind a highly similar motif (Bergsland et al., 2011; Heinz et al., 2010), activate an overlapping set of genes, and play a redundant function in pluripotency (Corsinotti et al., 2017; Niwa et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Both SOX2 and SOX3 are expressed in human ESCs but SOX3 was more specifically expressed in ESCs.
source: In addition, we observed that both SOX2 and SOX3 are expressed in human ESCs but SOX3 was more specifically expressed in ESCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, C).
evidence: This is supported by expression data analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: SOX2 binds preferentially 7up in a region coinciding with the 8 bp motif.
source: While SOX3 binding has not been profiled in human ESCs, ChIP-seq data available for SOX2 indicated that it binds preferentially 7up in a region coinciding with the 8 bp motif (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The 7d construct exhibited only weak promoter activity in iPSC compared to the empty vector.
source: The results of the assays revealed that the 7d construct exhibited, as predicted, only weak promoter activity in iPSC compared to the empty vector (Figure 6D), while the 7up1 construct had much stronger promoter activity, driving on average 7.8-fold more luciferase expression than 7d and 100-fold more than the empty vector (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The 7up1 construct had much stronger promoter activity, driving on average 7.8-fold more luciferase expression than 7d and 100-fold more than the empty vector.
source: The results of the assays revealed that the 7d construct exhibited, as predicted, only weak promoter activity in iPSC compared to the empty vector (Figure 6D), while the 7up1 construct had much stronger promoter activity, driving on average 7.8-fold more luciferase expression than 7d and 100-fold more than the empty vector (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The promoter activity was essentially abolished in the 7up1 construct lacking the 8 bp motif, which drove minimal luciferase expression (on average, 3-fold less than LTR7d and 20-fold less than the intact LTR7up sequence).
source: Strikingly, the promoter activity was essentially abolished in the 7up1 construct lacking the 8 bp motif, which drove minimal luciferase expression (on average, 3-fold less than LTR7d and 20-fold less than the intact LTR7up sequence).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The 8 bp motif in 7up1 is necessary for robust promoter activity in iPSCs, likely by providing a SOX2/3 binding site essential for this activity.
source: These results demonstrate that the 8 bp motif in 7up1 is necessary for robust promoter activity in iPSCs, likely by providing a SOX2/3 binding site essential for this activity.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6D and motif analysis.

claim: LTR7 is a polyphyletic group composed of at least eight monophyletic subfamilies.
source: In brief, our results show that: (i) LTR7 is a polyphyletic group composed of at least eight monophyletic subfamilies;
evidence: This is a summary of primary findings supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: LTR7 subfamilies have distinct evolutionary histories and transcriptional profiles in human embryos and a single and relatively small subgroup (~264 loci), LTR7up, exhibits robust promoter activity in ESC.
source: (ii) these subfamilies have distinct evolutionary histories and transcriptional profiles in human embryos and a single and relatively small subgroup (~264 loci), LTR7up, exhibits robust promoter activity in ESC;
evidence: This is a summary of primary findings supported by dating analysis (Figure 2), expression analysis (Figure 5), and regulatory analysis (Figure 3).

claim: LTR7 evolution is characterized by the gain, loss, and exchange of cis-regulatory modules likely underlying their transcriptional partitioning during early embryonic development.
source: (iii) LTR7 evolution is characterized by the gain, loss, and exchange of cis-regulatory modules likely underlying their transcriptional partitioning during early embryonic development.
evidence: This is a summary of primary findings supported by sequence analysis (Figure 4), motif analysis (Figure 6), and expression analysis (Figure 5).

claim: A phylogeny based on the coding sequence (reverse transcriptase [RVT] domain) of HERVH provided less granularity to separate the subfamilies than the LTR sequences.
source: Importantly, a phylogeny based on the coding sequence (reverse transcriptase [RVT] domain) of HERVH provided less granularity to separate the subfamilies than the LTR sequences (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 7u2 subfamily is the first subfamily of human TEs reported to have preimplantation expression exclusively in the epiblast.
source: For example, the 7u2 subfamily is, to our knowledge, the first subfamily of human TEs reported to have preimplantation expression exclusively in the epiblast.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: HERVH elements expressed in ESCs are almost exclusively driven by two closely related subfamilies of LTR7 (7up) that emerged most recently in hominoid evolution.
source: Our results provide an additional, perhaps simpler explanation: we found that HERVH elements expressed in ESCs are almost exclusively driven by two closely related subfamilies of LTR7 (7up) that emerged most recently in hominoid evolution.
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis (Figure 3) and dating analysis (Figure 2).

claim: The presence of a SOX2/3 site is not sufficient to confer transcriptional activity in ESC.
source: This exact motif is also present in the untranscribed 7u1 subfamily. More distantly related subfamilies also have SOX2/3 binding sites elsewhere on their sequence (Supplementary file 4), indicating that the presence of a SOX2/3 site is not sufficient to confer transcriptional activity in ESC.
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis and expression data comparison.

claim: The strength of the SOX2/3 motif match does not correlate with SOX2 binding or transcription within 7up.
source: Additionally, the strength of the motif match does not correlate with SOX2 binding or transcription within 7up (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Recombination is a common and important force in the evolution of exogenous RNA viruses and ERVs.
source: Recombination is a common and important force in the evolution of exogenous RNA viruses (Jetzt et al., 2000; Pérez-Losada et al., 2015; Simon-Loriere and Holmes, 2011) and ERVs (Vargiu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies proposed that the HERVH family had undergone inter-element recombination events of both its coding genes and LTR.
source: Previous studies proposed that the HERVH family had undergone inter-element recombination events of both its coding genes (Mager and Freeman, 1987; Vargiu et al., 2016) and LTR (Goodchild et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: It was inferred that recombination event between Type I LTR (i.e., LTR7) and Type II LTR (LTR7b) led to the emergence of Type Ia (LTR7y).
source: Specifically, it was inferred that recombination event between Type I LTR (i.e., LTR7) and Type II LTR (LTR7b) led to the emergence of Type Ia (LTR7y).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The coincidence of recombination events with changes in expression profiles suggests that these events were instrumental to the diversification of HERVH embryonic expression.
source: The coincidence of recombination events with changes in expression profiles (Figure 7) suggests that these events were instrumental to the diversification of HERVH embryonic expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between recombination events (Figure 4) and expression patterns (Figure 5) shown in Figure 7.

claim: The hybrid origin and subsequent burst of amplification of LTR7 subfamilies suggest they expanded rapidly after shifting their transcriptional profiles.
source: The hybrid origin and subsequent burst of amplification of LTR7 subfamilies (Figures 1 and 2) suggest they expanded rapidly after shifting their transcriptional profiles.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis (Figure 1) and dating analysis (Figure 2).

claim: Multiple HERVH subfamilies were transpositionally active in parallel during the past ~25 my of primate evolution.
source: Our evolutionary analysis reveals that multiple HERVH subfamilies were transpositionally active in parallel during the past ~25 my of primate evolution (Figures 2 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by dating analysis shown in Figures 2 and 7.

claim: The pattern of HERVH evolution is in stark contrast to the pattern of LINE1 evolution in primates, which is characterized by a single subfamily being predominantly active at any given time.
source: This is in stark contrast to the pattern of LINE1 evolution in primates, which is characterized by a single subfamily being predominantly active at any given time (Khan et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature on LINE1 evolution.

claim: Concurrently active HERVH subfamilies are transcribed at different developmental stages, such as 7up and 7u2 being transcribed in the pluripotent epiblast at the same time that 7y and the youngest 7b were transcribed at the 8 cell and morula stages.
source: Indeed, we observe that concurrently active HERVH subfamilies are transcribed at different developmental stages, such as 7up and 7u2 being transcribed in the pluripotent epiblast at the same time that 7y and the youngest 7b were transcribed at the 8 cell and morula stages (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis shown in Figure 5 and summarized in Figure 7.

claim: ZNF534 may repress 7up at earlier stages of development but is apparently unable to suppress 7up transcription in pluripotent stem cells.
source: Our analysis shows that ZNF534 is most highly expressed in the morula, but dips in human ESC (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). Thus, ZNF534 may repress 7up at earlier stages of development but is apparently unable to suppress 7up transcription in pluripotent stem cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on ZNF534 expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and its binding profile.

claim: HERVH/LTR7 has been used as a marker for human pluripotency.
source: HERVH/LTR7 has been used as a marker for human pluripotency (Ohnuki et al., 2014; Santoni et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014), and recent work has revealed that HERVH/LTR7-positive cells may be more amenable to differentiation, and are therefore referred to as 'primed' cells (Göke et al., 2015; Theunissen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HERVH/LTR7-positive cells may be more amenable to differentiation, and are therefore referred to as 'primed' cells.
source: HERVH/LTR7 has been used as a marker for human pluripotency (Ohnuki et al., 2014; Santoni et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014), and recent work has revealed that HERVH/LTR7-positive cells may be more amenable to differentiation, and are therefore referred to as 'primed' cells (Göke et al., 2015; Theunissen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous pan-LTR7 knockdown experiments have focused on highly transcribed LTR7 in primed ESCs and have primarily, if not exclusively, targeted 7up elements.
source: Previous pan-LTR7 knockdown experiments have focused on highly transcribed LTR7 in primed ESCs (Lu et al., 2014; Ohnuki et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2012). As such, these experiments have primarily, if not exclusively, targeted 7up elements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that 7up elements are the primary transcribed LTR7 in ESCs and citations to previous knockdown studies.

claim: While 7up shows expression preference in primed cell lines, 7u2 shows preference for naïve lines.
source: Indeed, while 7up shows expression preference in primed cell lines, 7u2 shows preference for naïve lines (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Elements of the 7u2 subfamily are highly and exclusively expressed in the pluripotent epiblast in vivo but weakly so in H1 ESC, which consists of a majority of primed cells and a minority of naïve or formative cells.
source: Of relevance to this issue is our finding that elements of the 7u2 subfamily are highly and exclusively expressed in the pluripotent epiblast in vivo (Figure 5), but weakly so in H1 ESC, which consists of a majority of primed cells and a minority of naïve or formative cells (Gafni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis shown in Figure 5 and a citation to previous literature on H1 ESC composition.
